books.section: Topic 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification
Topic 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification, C. Federalists, Anti-Federalists, and the Adoption of the Bill of Rights

primary_sources: George Mason, Objections to the Constitution of Government formed by the Convention (September 1787)
George Washington to James Madison, November 5, 1786
Massachusetts Ratifying Convention, Form of Ratification (February 6, 1788)
Ratification votes of the state conventions, 1787-1790

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the debates over ratification of the Constitution reflected competing visions of republican government in the period 1787–1791.

documents.title: Publius (James Madison), Federalist No. 10
documents.source: Publius (James Madison), Federalist No. 10, New York Daily Advertiser, November 22, 1787. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A newspaper essay by Madison, written as Publius to persuade New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution.
documents.text: “By a faction, I understand a number of citizens, whether amounting to a majority or a minority of the whole, who are united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adversed to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community. . . . Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens.”

documents.title: Brutus, No. 1
documents.source: Brutus, No. 1, New-York Journal, October 18, 1787. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An Anti-Federalist essay, written under a pseudonym for New York readers weighing ratification.
documents.text: “The first question that presents itself on the subject is, whether a confederated government be the best for the United States or not? Or in other words, whether the thirteen United States should be reduced to one great republic, governed by one legislature, and under the direction of one executive and judicial; or whether they should continue thirteen confederated republics, under the direction and controul of a supreme federal head for certain defined national purposes only? . . . This government is to possess absolute and uncontroulable power, legislative, executive and judicial, with respect to every object to which it extends.”

documents.title: Publius, Federalist No. 51
documents.source: Publius, Federalist No. 51, February 1788. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Federalist essay defending the Constitution's structure to New York readers during ratification.
documents.text: “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition. . . . If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controuls on government would be necessary. In framing a government which is to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to controul the governed; and in the next place, oblige it to controul itself.”

documents.title: George Mason's Objections to the Constitution
documents.source: George Mason, Objections to the Constitution of Government formed by the Convention, September 1787. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A memorandum by a Virginia delegate who refused to sign, circulated to persuade others against the document.
documents.text: “There is no Declaration of Rights; and the Laws of the general Government being paramount to the Laws & Constitution of the several States, the Declarations of Rights in the separate States are no Security. . . . In the House of Representatives there is not the Substance, but the Shadow only of Representation. . . . There is no Declaration of any kind for preserving the Liberty of the Press, the Tryal by jury in civil Causes; nor against the Danger of standing Armies in time of Peace.”

documents.title: George Washington to James Madison
documents.source: George Washington to James Madison, Mount Vernon, November 5, 1786. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A private letter from Washington, written as Shays's Rebellion alarmed national leaders.
documents.text: “Without some alteration in our political creed, the superstructure we have been seven years raising at the expence of much blood and treasure, must fall. We are fast verging to anarchy and confusion! . . . Thirteen sovereignties pulling against each other, and all tugging at the Federal head, will soon bring ruin on the whole; whereas a liberal and energetic Constitution, well guarded and closely watched, to prevent encroachments, might restore us to that degree of respectability and consequence, to which we are entitled.”

documents.title: Massachusetts Ratifying Convention: Ratification and Recommended Amendments
documents.source: Massachusetts Ratifying Convention, Form of Ratification, February 6, 1788. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The form by which Massachusetts ratified, with recommended amendments attached to win over opponents.
documents.text: “The Convention, having impartially discussed and fully considered the Constitution for the United States of America . . . do, in the name and in behalf of the people of the commonwealth of Massachusetts, assent to and ratify the said Constitution for the United States of America. And, as it is the opinion of this Convention, that certain amendments and alterations in the said Constitution would remove the fears and quiet the apprehensions of many of the good people of the commonwealth . . . the Convention do therefore recommend that the following alterations and provisions be introduced into the said Constitution: First. That it be explicitly declared, that all powers not expressly delegated by the aforesaid Constitution are reserved to the several states, to be by them exercised.”

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the ratification debates reflected competing visions of republican government, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation, Shays's Rebellion, or the fear of distant authority after British rule.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument about competing visions of republican government.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents from both the Federalist and the Anti-Federalist sides.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six from one side only, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as Patrick Henry's attack on We the People at the Virginia convention, the three delegates who refused to sign, or the Bill of Rights ratified in 1791.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument, such as the Federalist essays written to win New York, Brutus writing under a pseudonym, or Mason's objections as a refusal to sign.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where the two visions shared ground, or weighing which vision won and what it cost, as in the promised Bill of Rights.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The ratification debates reflected two competing visions of republican government to a great extent, because Federalists and Anti-Federalists disagreed over whether liberty was safer in a large republic with checks or in small republics close to the people, though both sides claimed to defend liberty and the Bill of Rights closed the gap.
Context: The Articles of Confederation had left Congress unable to tax, raise troops, or stop Shays's Rebellion, and nationalists called for a stronger government while many Americans still feared distant authority after British rule.
Federalist vision: Document 1 shows Madison arguing that an extended republic controls faction by taking in more interests. Document 3 shows the checks-and-balances answer: ambition checks ambition, and government must both govern and restrain itself. Document 5 shows Washington calling for a liberal and energetic Constitution.
Anti-Federalist vision: Document 2 shows Brutus warning that the Constitution would reduce thirteen confederated republics to one great republic. Document 4 shows Mason's first objection, the missing declaration of rights, and his warning that federal law would override state protections.
The fight and its settlement: Document 6 shows Massachusetts ratifying only with recommended amendments attached. Document 7 shows the pattern: small states ratified quickly and unanimously, while Massachusetts, Virginia, and New York were slow and nearly tied.
Beyond the documents: Patrick Henry attacked We the People at the Virginia convention, three delegates refused to sign at Philadelphia, and the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791.
Complexity: The visions shared the language of liberty and the fear of tyranny, and the Federalist victory was conditioned on the Bill of Rights, so the debate ended in a bargain rather than a rout.
